 The 7 Things You Must Check in a Purchase Agreement Before Buying an Accounting Firm
Hi Sara,
If you’re buying an accounting practice, you’re going to come across a purchase agreement—and let’s be real, it will probably look like a 20-page legal maze designed to put you to sleep. 
But here’s the thing: this document controls everything about your deal. It’s your business’s user manual, your playbook, and, if something goes wrong, your only protection.
So today, I’m breaking down the seven key sections you must understand before signing on the dotted line.
1. What Exactly Are You Buying? (And What’s Excluded?)
This is where you find out if you’re getting all the assets you expect—or if the seller conveniently forgot to include key client lists, software, or equipment. If you’re the buyer, you want the contract to say everything is included unless specifically excluded. If you’re the seller? You want the opposite.
2. The Money Details (a.k.a. The Purchase Price)
How much are you paying?

Is it all cash, or is there a promissory note?

Are there any earnout term or price adjustments based on client retention or revenue?

Miss something here, and you might be in for a nasty surprise later.
3. Closing Mechanics: When Does This Deal Actually Happen?
Most deals aren’t “sign today, close today.” They involve a bifurcated sign-and-close, meaning:
✔ You sign the agreement now.
✔ The deal officially closes later—after financing, approvals, or other conditions are met.
If you don’t structure this properly, you could be legally obligated to buy before securing funding. (Yes, I’ve seen this happen. Yes, it got ugly.)
4. The Seller’s Promises (And Why They Matter)
Reps and warranties are the seller’s legal promises about the business. Things like:
“Our financial statements are accurate.”

“We actually own the assets we’re selling.”

“We haven’t secretly sold the client list to someone else.”

If any of these turn out to be false, you’ve got a breach of contract claim. But only if you made sure they were included in writing. These are SUPER important.
5. What Happens If Something Goes Wrong?
This is where indemnification comes in—it decides who pays if a lawsuit shows up later.
Example: A client sues over work done before closing.

Who’s responsible—you or the seller?

Get this section wrong, and you could be on the hook for past problems you had nothing to do with.
6. Non-Compete Clauses (The Fine Print That Matters)
If you’re the buyer, you don’t want the seller setting up shop across the street and poaching clients. If you’re the seller, you don’t want to be banned from your entire profession for the next decade.
The right non-compete is a balance—clear, enforceable, and specific. If it’s too broad, courts might throw it out. If it’s too narrow, it won’t protect you. If you’re the one under a non-compete, you’re going to want it to be specific enough that you can tell whether or not a business opportunity will violate it.
7. The Boilerplate (Yes, You Still Have to Read It)
The last section might seem like legal fluff, but I’ve found some wild clauses buried in here—like secret fees, weird assignment rules, and even clauses that completely contradict earlier sections. So read it.
The Bottom Line
A purchase agreement is more than just paperwork—it’s the foundation of your deal. If you don’t understand what’s in it, you’re flying blind.

This is what I do every day, and trust me—you don’t want to find out what’s missing in your contract when it’s already too late.
To smarter deals,
Sara Sharp
